If you have a Kindle, seriously consider subscribing to Kindle Unlimited, especially if you devour books at the rate I do. It's basically a lending library, allowing you to download 10 books at a time. If you're reading a 2-3-or-4- book set, and you're ready to move to the next in the series, you must have fewer than 10 loaded. But all you need do is Return one or more of the titles you have already read, and you can then load the same number of new titles into your Kindle.

The creators of Kindle and the new Kindle Unlimited seem to just keep coming up with better and better ideas!

Kindle owners who like to read in bed but their mate minds the reading light will definitely want the Kindle Paperwhite, with its adjustable backlighting options. Never glare-y, just perfect. If my current Paperwhite dies some day, I will thank it for its service, then, after an appropriate moment of silence, will race to the laptop to order another.

Keep up the great work, Kindlemakers!!

I like the clips a lot. I have a lot of things on my desk so that means a lot of USB cables. Before the cables would slide off the desk or get tangled up … now they are all neat and organized. No more falling off the desk, either, since the cable clips hold the cords in place.

The cable clips are designed for computer and phone charging cables, anything 8mm in diameter or less. HDMI cables, thick power cables, and the like won’t fit into the cable clips. The product description states this, so I’m not complaining, I just wanted to mention it.

text_fidelity_a: WYZE Cam 1080p HD Indoor Smart Home Camera with Night Vision, 2-Way Audio, Compatible with Alexa & the Google Assistant Bulbs and outlet are OK. I would not buy separately though, as nowadays you get higher quality bulbs and outlets for a discount price.  The sensor bridge, contact and motion sensors are problematic to say the least. I have 2 contact sensors and 3 motion sensors connected to the sensor bridge. Right now all of them are offline, they started going offline one by one. Distance from the sensors to the bridge is not an issue since two of them are located no more than three feet away from the bridge. This is not the first time this has happened. The only solution for me has been to reset bridge and sensors, and reinstall them one by one. Many people complain about the same issue, and this keeps happening. The camera where the bridge is attached is installed 7 ft from the ground, so it has been very aggravating to have to get a ladder every time one of these switches has gone offline. Regarding the camera, you probably will not find anything cheaper in the market right now. This model in particular offers continuous recording provided you insert a storage card, that is a plus. Person detection is back, however sometimes it takes more than 10 minutes to receive a notification. Some people has reported that it has take up to one hour to get the notification. I personally would not recommend getting this package due to the unreliability of the bridge and motion and contact sensors. This is definitely not a system you want to buy to secure your home. The camera can be purchased separately for about $25. The video quality is acceptable during the daytime. If you want a hobby camera, you will not find a better deal. For security purposes, you are better off looking somewhere else.
text_fidelity_b: WYZE Cam 1080p HD Indoor Smart Home Camera with Night Vision, 2-Way Audio, Compatible with Alexa & the Google Assistant

It's always been my opinion that pre-built machines focus on the specs of a few key components and then skimp on the rest. I can't say this machine changed my mind on that, but it is nice for most people, who don't want to figure out how to make their own to have something already together that just works.

So far, I've used it for a few months and haven't had any failures. It's handled software installations, Windows updates, and new hardware with a minimum of errors. The card readers work. The ports are easy to reach. it isn't especially noisy, but it's far from silent. I've used it for mild gaming, some CAD design work with a program that often crashes and is a ram-hog, and general browing and have had no lagging or problems. Seems to work great!

In my haste to get rid of pre-installed software, I removed the software that turns the light in the DELL logo on and off on the front. I had turned it off, but as soon as I rebooted, it came on and stayed that way. The wires don't seem to be easily accessible to unplug it. I don't consider a bright blue glowing logo that defaults to on to be an added value to the customer, but I guess I'm not really surprised.

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin Portable Friction Mount - Frustration Free Packaging The frustration free packaging is a big plus.
The mount itself is perfect for our needs.
We have a Garmin Nuvi which came with the window suction mount. The window mount has a ball-joint the same as this friction mount.
The GPS came with the clip-on bracket which has the socket attached which then clips onto the ball on this friction mount.
This forms a multi-directional ball and socket joint allowing for easy angle adjustments.

This mount has stayed in place with no problems, even when we've armorall'ed the dashboard. Then again, we don't fling the truck around like teenagers either, the worst we do is bounce it around on some dirt roads.

We much prefer this over the window mount for several reasons:
We live in Georgia (USA) and the heat and the humidity in summer takes its toll on the sucker attachments on the window mounts.
For security, we move the GPS from sight whenever we park.... the whole unit is easily picked up and placed on the floor.
We couldn't do this with a window mount. We either unclipped and left the mount attached to the window, a visible tell-tale that there's a GPS in the vehicle. Or, we would fiddle to remove the whole mount from the window (never too easy), and then are left with a tell-tale suction scum ring on the window! ...once more telling would-be GPS thieves that there's a GPS in the car! And that scum ring is just unsightly. Yes, you can get wipes... but this is a far more elegant solution and much more convenient.
Recommended.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin Portable Friction Mount - Frustration Free Packaging

text_fidelity_a:
Cisco-Linksys E3000 Wireless-N Router I bought this router in December, 2010 to replace my Linksys WRT54GS wireless router. I was a bit surprised to find that there are no external antennae and no place to install one on the E3000, but I haven't encountered any problems with signal. This router hasn't bottlenecked once, whereas my WRT54GS would bottleneck if the wind blew wrong. The only time I have unplugged this router was because I had to reconfigure it from scratch when I discovered I couldn't configure any of the settings using the built-in software once I'd changed the router configuration in the browser config pages. I read some work-arounds in the Amazon.com reviews and had to reset to factory defaults. I had to fully uninstall and reinstall the Cisco Connect software as well. As long as you go through that software first and THEN make adjustments in your advanced configuration settings via your web browser, you can still access things like parental control and guest wifi security. If you change your router's address, however, from 192.168.1.1 to anything different, expect to never be able to get into Cisco Connect again. The only reason I can envision needing the Cisco Connect software is to access the guest wifi and the parental controls, so if you don't need those things, don't worry about making changes you normally would via the browser interface.

The wifi button on the router is handy for setting up wireless devices such as cell phones and internet tablets, it hooks right up to your wireless network and you don't have to rely on the guest access to connect. You will also have the ability to set up a physical key using a USB thumb drive (you must provide your own) for setting up other computers on your wifi network, which works like a charm. It is especially compatible with the Cisco-Linksys WUSB600N Dual-Band Wireless-N USB Network Adapter, which I also highly recommend. I haven't tried the networked storage option yet due to the location of my router in relation to my external drives, but it is definitely an option that I will look into setting up some day.

I would say this router is worth the $150 I paid for it (locally), with the biggest reason being that so far I haven't been able to bottleneck it, even with my 60MB cable service, wireless-connected computers, Wii, and other various wireless devices. Cisco/Linksys really did a good thing with this model and I'm quite pleased with it; it is definitely worth the price.
text_fidelity_b: Cisco-Linksys E3000 Wireless-N Router

BRAINWAVZ S0 in-Ear Earbuds Noise Isolating Earphones Clearwavz Remote & Microphone Stereo Headphone Headset for iPhone iPad, iPod & Android Devices (Black) I love how comfortable these ear buds are. I’ve always been pleased with Brainwavz earphone comfort, but these have raised the comfort bar even higher. I’m using it mainly with the tri-flange tips which I’ve tried with other headphones but didn't care that much for. With the S0's, however, the tri-flange fit very well, provide for good sound isolation, and stay put even when I’m on the treadmill. Very well done.

The sound quality is also quite pleasing. There’s ample bass without it being boomy or muddy. Just a nice, solid low-frequency response that sounds great. The mid-range is clear even at higher volumes. The only small shortfall is with the upper ranges, which are not as clear and sharp as they could be, and get somewhat shrill at high volumes. But at normal volumes it’s a nicely balanced sound, and considering the price, I would describe the sound quality as very good overall.

The build quality feels pretty solid. The cables are well-attached and have molded connectors at the ear buds to give it better durability. That’s important for me since, while this comes with a very nice carry case, I usually just wrap the cords around whatever device I’m using, which puts a lot of stress on the connectors. These feel more than solid enough to deal with that level of abuse. I have a few other Brainwavz earphones and have yet to have one fail on me.

This is well worth a spot on your short list if you’re shopping for a well-made, comfortable set of earbuds that deliver solid sound without breaking the bank. Highly recommend.

Logitech G502 Proteus Spectrum RGB Tunable Gaming Mouse, 12,000 DPI On-The-Fly DPI Shifting, Personalized Weight and Balance Tuning with (5) 3.6g Weights, 11 Programmable Buttons I’m not a hardcore gamer anymore, so for the past few years, I’ve been using a Logitech M570 Wireless Trackball (thumb trackball). I like trackballs for everyday use, and it’s adequate for casual World of Warcraft playing. Most of the time I just futz around leveling alts or doing 5 mans with friends.

But lately I’ve been wanting a mouse I can customize, with more options to adjust my playstyle. It’s cold in my house in the winter, so I wanted to set up mouseover macros and use more mouse buttons, because my hands are cold sitting on the keyboard. So the G502 Proteus Spectrum seemed like a good mouse to review.

I just had one problem: my computer can’t customize the mouse. Why? I have a Mac Book Air.

Now, I know the G502 says on the box that it supports Windows. There’s no mention of Mac support. But I’ve never had a problem with my Mac recognizing Logitech mice, so I figured I’d be safe. What I didn’t know is that Logitech gaming mice have separate software from the Logitech Control Center for regular Logitech mice.

After some Googling, I found the Logitech Gaming Software, which supports Mac OS X 10.8.x and up. I installed it on a Mavericks machine and a Yosemite machine. Neither computer’s Logitech Gaming Software was able to find the mouse. The G502 Proteus CORE is supported, but not the G502 Proteus SPECTRUM.

So right now, I’m unable to customize any of the extra buttons or RGB lighting or any of the other special features. It’s a really fancy basic mouse. I will continue to check for Proteus Spectrum support in the Mac Logitech Gaming Center, and update this review when I can customize things. I’m going into so much detail on the Mac side of things because I know I’m not the only Mac person who tried to use this mouse. I think there’s a workaround with Bootcamp or using a Windows computer, but I’m unable to try that.

I did use the mouse for a few weeks, to test the comfort. I’m really picky on how mice feel in my hand. I’m female and have smaller hands. I like how this mouse didn’t feel too short, and it wasn’t too heavy or wide for me to use comfortably for hours at a time. I also liked the included weights, so you can adjust the weight of the mouse. I haven’t had a mouse with an adjustable weight before, and I liked that extra level of customization.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech G502 Proteus Spectrum RGB Tunable Gaming Mouse, 12,000 DPI On-The-Fly DPI Shifting, Personalized Weight and Balance Tuning with (5) 3.6g Weights, 11 Programmable Buttons

text_fidelity_a:
Canon Cameras US PowerShot SX720 HS Black My SX280 HS is becoming unreliable, throwing E32 lens errors. This is the closest replacement, AFAIK. The 40x zoom is probably not that useful, since the 280's 20x was right at the limit of stable framing, but no biggie. I just like the SX HS series with the DIGIC 6 processor. I looked at the 730, but didn't need Bluetooth & didn't like the look of the oversimplified controls. And $50 buys a couple of extra batteries.

One thing you do get for several years of technology development is a better battery/sensor. Thus far the 720 shows no sign of gobbling electricity the way the 280 does. The extra $100 also buys a better written manual. I discovered a couple of minor features both cameras have, but which you'd be hard pressed to figure out from the 280's manual.--9/2/2017
Update: The 280's video/battery life problems are fixed in the 720. Image stabilization is very good. I got acceptable results at >20x zoom with a light-weight monopod (a Slik). Close focus also appears much better.--9/4/2017
I'm still on my first battery charge!--9/17/2017
Update: I fixed the 280's lens errors with a can of air and a heavy hand blowing out the gaps in the lens. Risky, but it worked. The 720 is still my go to camera. I upped the rating to 5.
July 2019 Update--I got a killer deal on a Panasonic Lumix ZS70. Great camera ... but ... it feels a lot bigger than this one in my hand. It has more features, does more things, but the 720 is lighter, handier, and in some cases takes better still pictures. If you don't need an EVF, tilt-screen and better video, this (or its SX740HS successor) might just be the better choice. The 740 has a tilt-screen.
June 2020
One word of advice. The sensor is 20 Mpx. The lens is capable of delivering 5-8 Mpx. This is typical of these small cameras. Don't be afraid to use lower resolutions or higher compressions. You won't lose much. Still a favorite camera.
text_fidelity_b: Canon Cameras US PowerShot SX720 HS Black

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Basics Wireless Bluetooth Fitness Headphones Earbuds with Microphone, Black Short story of the review is that these are just as they say they are--a pair of relatively inexpensive "basic" earphones. As such, they seem to be a decent value and have some good points, but if you're looking for sound quality over price, you'll want to go elsewhere.

Pros:
Packaging: small and minimalist as it should be

Provided with: multiple size earbuds caps and ear inserts (more on these later), a very short charging cable, and a decent zip-around traveling pouch

Pairing: No problem with any of my Apple devices. Instantly recognized and paired with an iPhone (8 and 6), iPad (Pro and Air 2), and MacBook Pro. Couldn't be quicker or easier each and every time

Comfort: This was an issue for me, though obviously this is a pretty subjective category. I had to step down immediately to the small caps/rings, which is no surprise--I do that with I think all of my earbuds. But even with the smalls I just couldn't get a a good seal or a comfortable, though oddly enough much worse with my right. The left was not "great" but was certainly good; right was a bad seal and wholly uncomfortable no matter what I tried. Weird.

Sound quality: Again, it's a matter of pricing here. I don't own many basics and it's been years since I've had a set of lower-tier earbuds, so it's hard for me to compare at an equal level. The sound is what I'd call adequate, especially for exercise or listening to an audiobook. But there's no comparison to my PowerBeats3 or Jaybird X2s, and not even to my Jabra Elites, which I"d call my mid-range ones. The first two are in a whole other class in terms of range, sharpness, richness, and comfort, while the Jabras are a good step up in both sound and comfort. Sound here is more than a little thin at both ends, and just not very rich or full. Less noticeable with an audiobook, but definitely not the buds I'd choose if I'm focusing on listening to music, as opposed to having background sound while I"m doing something else. Phone quality is pretty similar--adequate, at times a bit muddy.

Controls: easy, intuitive, and responsive

Overall, if you want a basic set where quality of sound isn't a deal breaker, or a pair of cheaper ones for places you might have to worry about forgetting them, these will suit the bill, assuming you don't have the same comfort issue I did. But for someone looking for rich, full sound, particularly for music, I'd strongly advise moving up the ladder
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Basics Wireless Bluetooth Fitness Headphones Earbuds with Microphone, Black

text_fidelity_a:
Brainwavz R3 Dual Dynamic Driver Earphones (V2) I use earbuds a lot since I typically prefer the lightness and ease of use compared with traditional headphones. Right out of the box these were a bit puzzling as to how to position them for use. But, after a bit of fiddling with the over-the-ear loop, it becomes clear.

The in-ear comfort is good. It comes with a variety of ear tips including two types I’ve not used before: a double flange silicon tip and a triple flange silicon tip. The flanges allow the ear bud to make a much better seal in your ear canal. That not only helps cut out ambient noise intruding, it also improves the bass response. I found the double flange works best for me, but the variety of tips included appears sufficient to fit pretty much any ear.

It also comes with an excellent case for storage, and adapters for airplane use and for 1/4 inch plugs. I especially like the case since it’s small enough to make it easy to carry along (roughly 3.5 inches by 3 by 1.5 inches thick) and is reinforced to avoid being crushed. It has mesh pockets to keep everything stowed, and looks nice to boot (black with red contrast in the middle). All-in-all, it’s a great kit in terms of useful accessories.

I’m not as pleased with the cord. While I like how sturdy it is, it has a “Y” link that always seems to be in the way when I’m working out. I got used to it eventually, but a more streamlined cord system would have been a better design approach. Another negative is the 3.5mm plug. It needs to be seated just so or you get sound cut-outs or static. I tried it with several devices to be sure the issue is with the plug and not the device. A more robust plug is needed for this – you shouldn’t have to fiddle with it to get it to seat properly.

The over-the-ear loops are also a bit annoying at first. Granted, that’s certainly due to the fact that I usually use standard in-ear buds without the loop, so any type of loop feels weird to me at first. The material is soft and bendy, so you can position it in any variety of ways. It could benefit from some additional padding. On the plus side, they do hold the buds in very well. Quick head movements that would have loosened an in-ear bud didn’t jar these loose at all.

Now for the really important feature: how they sound. In a word, excellent. My benchmark for moderately-priced earbuds has been units made by RHA out of the UK. These sound nearly as good. Very clean sound but still ample bass provided that you select the right tip. For me, the standard tip (the one installed as delivered) gave me very little in terms of bass. Selecting a different tip to provide a better ear fit did wonders for bass response.

They are a bit more airy than the RHA sound. That could be a plus or a minus depending on your preferred type of music. Very heavy bass music is not a good match for these. Pretty much everything else is, and I appreciated the enhanced clarity. It’s the type of sound that, when you hear it, the first word that would come to mind is “clean.”

They look odd, make take you a moment to figure out how to position them, but provide a very open, natural sound. It comes with a well-designed kit of useful extras. However, the plug issues, the cord, and the ear loops collectively knock it down a star. Still well worth considering, however, and I would certainly recommend them.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Brainwavz R3 Dual Dynamic Driver Earphones (V2)

text_fidelity_a:
Blink Whole Home Bundle | Video Doorbell System, Outdoor camera, and Mini camera | HD video, motion detection, Works with Alexa "Set up in minutes"?? Not really. There are no actual detailed instructions included. I tried scanning the QR code that was provided in the little pamphlet, and that was not helpful. This ended up being extremely frustrating to set up. I could take a wild guess that I was supposed put the lithium batteries in the back of the camera. I would not have known that the little QR code inside the camera where the batteries go was something that I had to scan to set up the camera. Anyway, without going into detail, if Amazon provided some simple, basic instructions with photos that show step by step, it would save the customer a ton of fumbling around. Then it might have been an easy set up. I had to call for support, and by the time I got a support person on the phone I was pretty irritated. The reason I decided to buy this camera is the "two-year battery life." Note: these are not rechargeable batteries. We'll see how long the batteries last. Prior to this, I got a Eufy Solocam, also wireless (and much, much easier to set up), and it had rechargeable batteries advertised to last 4 months, but they lasted 4 weeks. A feature that is missing with the Blink camera, that I liked on the Eufy camera, is the AI feature to recognize humans. Without the AI feature, the Blink is recording non-human motion, such as animals and vehicles.

Update: The description advertises customized zones for motion detection. The camera takes a photo what it sees, and in motion settings, you gray out areas that you do not want the camera to detect motion. It does NOT work. I tried resetting it several times, and the camera recorded and sent me an alert of motion detected that was squarely in the grayed out area. Without this feature actually working, and without the AI feature to detect humans, the camera is recording every motion in the entire viewable area, ignoring the areas that I grayed out. I am returning this camera.
text_fidelity_b: Blink Whole Home Bundle | Video Doorbell System, Outdoor camera, and Mini camera | HD video, motion detection, Works with Alexa

text_fidelity_a:
Yamaha AVENTAGE RX-A880 7.2-ch 4K Ultra HD AV Receiver with HDR Dolby Vision Dolby Atmos Wi-Fi Phono YPAO and MusicCast. Works with Alexa. Update: I really love this machine. You give a lot of things five stars if they're really good products, but this one deserves bonus. I've been slowly going through the full 200+ page manual to make sure I don't miss any features and to get the most out of this thing, and I'm continually thrilled. Also, I give a lot of things controlled by apps low ratings because I tend to hate screwing around with my phone, but in this case, the Yamaha AV controller app only adds to the value, with the best part being you don't NEED it to take advantage of all the receiver's functionality, but it's a joy to have sometimes to make fine adjustments without having to turn on the TV. I really like it for adjusting net radio stations and stuff like that or fine tuning music sounds - again, without having to turn on the TV. This also makes up for the one negative I mentioned below about not being able to change all the settings from a web page. Great stuff!

Original review:

Before this, I had two Sony receivers in my living room. My secondary is a much older model - about 12 or so years old - that does not have HDMI and I use it for my whole house audio system. My primary is (was - it just got replaced) a 3-5 year old Sony model that is admittedly in a lower class than this Yamaha receiver (the secondary was in a higher class in its time, I think).

While I usually have all Sony stuff, I was completely willing to try another well-known Japanese brand who specializes in receivers and amps. And - it's just awesome. Totally. Not a single regret about the switch. The RX-A880 gave me back everything I lost going from my older, higher-end Sony to my newer one, AND it gave me so many nice surprises on the way! As anyone can tell you that it sounds good and looks good, I'll concentrate on this little details that I discovered during setup:

1) Besides the seven HDMI inputs, it also has a composite video, a component video, two optical audio, one extra (second belongs to component) coax audio, and two composite audio inputs, not to mention phono.

The great thing is that you can assign different audio inputs to any of the video inputs. So, for example, I decided to keep my Wii around since I now have a component input (and it takes up almost no space), but the cable is component video with composite audio, but the component video input on this has coax for the audio. Bummer. But no, you can change it. Example number two is I have a computer in my telecom closet hooked up to this with both HDMI and line-out audio. For circumstances too complicated to define here, audio does not output via the HDMI. But because of this feature, I can make the audio appear when I select the HDMI input OR when I just want to listen to the audio directly (with no HDMI output). Perfect.

2) 9 Speaker outputs. First, I'm so happy to have the 2-zone thing back (my secondary receiver has it, but my other, newer Sony did not - it only had A/B speakers that shared an amp). But this one you can actually have 7.1 AND a second zone (although you can't play them at the same time. This is really cool if you want the best of both worlds. I don't know if I can find a place for two more speakers in my setup, but ...it's nice to have the option. Supposedly, this all works automatically. I imagine it could work fine, but I am unable to try it at the moment.

3) 2-zone done better. My older Sony had 2-zone, but the controls were - frankly - atrocious. It was always confusing, even for someone like me who can be a super A/V nerd and memorize anything. The way I use it now is just to keep the remote on Zone-2, and do Zone-1 on the unit itself.

This Yamaha, however, has a simple switch on the remote, and you're either controlling one zone or the other depending on that switch. Simple and effective. You can also control it from the unit, unlike the older Sony.

4) 8 custom presets, all controlled directly from the remote. Another 8 for Zone 2?!

The one complaint I read by a reviewer was that you have to scroll through all the inputs from the remote to get to what you want. But that doesn't matter for two reasons: first, you can change the settings to skip anything you don't want. But, second, with 8 custom presets - and each with their own remote button - you probably don't even ever need to scroll through the inputs anyway.

And the custom presets are great. You can turn on and off a bunch of features like whether or not it changes your HDMI out settings, if it uses your YPAO settings, extra bass, which speakers it uses, etc. And it even can link the second zone!

Two great examples:

I can't stand to watch regular background TV with the surround sound on because it makes the commercials that much more obnoxious. But of course I like big booming bass and surround for movies. And it's also annoying to switch the unit off and on all the time, especially if you want to use control for HDMI. So I have one preset for very flat TV sound using just the front speakers that is clearer than-, but no more annoying than-, my regular TV speakers. Then I have another preset for surround sound and big bass for movie watching.

I have one preset for straight music just in zone 1. Then I have another preset for straight music in both zones one and two. It turns on zone 2 automatically. I could not figure out how to make a preset just for zone 2, but it seems that when I am controlling zone 2 on the remote, I can make 8 more presets just for zone 2. You can not adjust these presets via menu, from what I can tell, though.

5) 14 character names on the front of the unit in dot matrix. My other receivers were all limited to 8 characters. You can see all 14 at once, which is great.

6) Much more robust networking. I haven't played with this too awful much yet, but it seems that if you start listening to a playlist or an album on your NAS, then the next time you go back to "server", it will start playing where you left off (well, the song you left off at will start over again, instead of at the exact moment you left at), but at least this way you don't have to turn the TV on just to play some music. I suppose you could create a playlist of all Death Metal, and then you just have a stream going whenever you want it. It also seems like you can actually sign into Pandora and all the other stations and listen to your own account. And all the Internet/Network stuff is a separate scroll-through than the other inputs. I really like how that is set up.

6) The "program up/down" buttons on the remote can be programmed to do about 10 different things. I picked to have the dialogue increased or decreased for when you can't hear what people are saying even though everything else is loud enough. To be clear, I think this depends on if the dialogue is known to the decoder. I haven't tried all the other options yet.

7) Remote is awesome. Besides what I mentioned above, you can also make some changes to the red/green/yellow/blue buttons, but I wish you could really program those completely to your liking. Everything is laid out nicely, and the second zone even makes sense, as I mentioned above.

8) I realize the second HDMI output would be great if you also have a projector or something like that. With it, you can have access to all your devices without having to rewire anything. Haven't used it yet, but am glad to have the extra functionality.

...

There's plenty more, but I'm forgetting some of the details right now. I've only played with this thing for a few days, but I like it more and more. The one thing that is missing is that you can't change all the options via the webpage. You can change some, but I liked with my newer Sony the fact that I could look at and change all my custom presets without having to turn the TV and go through all that. I'm only comparing this to my two Sony units so you get my frame of reference, but realize this Yamaha model is in a higher class than those. Regardless, I love this thing, and it has a lot of great functionality and no serious drawbacks that I've noticed yet. Recommended (obviously).
text_fidelity_b: Yamaha AVENTAGE RX-A880 7.2-ch 4K Ultra HD AV Receiver with HDR Dolby Vision Dolby Atmos Wi-Fi Phono YPAO and MusicCast. Works with Alexa.

text_fidelity_a:
Bestlight 48 LED Macro Ring Light With 6 Adaptors Rings for Canon Digital EOS Rebel SL1 (100D),T5i(700D),T4i(650D),T3(1100D),T3i(600D),60D,60Da,50D,Nikon D5300,D5000,D3000,D3200,D5100 DSLR Cameras 48 LED unit - (since several items are listed under one product ID)
Positives:
- It is what it looks like, does what it claims to do, and basically works
- cheap
- comes with an AC adapter!! Wow. You can pay a lot for a light that doesn't

Negatives: I'm using this for Macro work (I'm new to macro) so that's the perspective I'm coming from
- Not Bright Enough! It's just not all that bright. Not enough to light a subject by itself for macro purposes. I doubt it's adequate for more than a highlight for portraiture. This is why 2 stars. If a light doesn't light - it's not a light.

Really that's it. This is not a knock to the light (and not why I gave it a low rating), but if you are planning on using it for macro, buy a flash instead. A flash will not only have higher output, but will help freeze the camera shake (a big macro problem). Also, I thought the full time light would be better for live insects (you can see what you're doing!), but it's the opposite. You need the flash to freeze action. Not a criticism (this light does not advertise itself as a flash), but something to know.

UPDATE: I used it a couple more times. I am finding it more useful than initially when very close in. I would still strongly recommend a flash for this unless you have a compelling reason for continuous illumination (e.g you're waiting for a bug to crawl into frame and it's too dark to see otherwise. Though the lights would probably scare the bug). If you have a pretty solid tripod setup, this can work for longer exposure macro. Not great though. Upped to 3 stars.
text_fidelity_b: Bestlight 48 LED Macro Ring Light With 6 Adaptors Rings for Canon Digital EOS Rebel SL1 (100D),T5i(700D),T4i(650D),T3(1100D),T3i(600D),60D,60Da,50D,Nikon D5300,D5000,D3000,D3200,D5100 DSLR Cameras

Fortunately it fits just barely in my Sentey Gaming case. I had purchased the Arctic Freezer 7 Pro Rev 2 but that was far worse than the AMD 8350's included cooler fan, probably because the contact surface is designed for Intel chips and is much smaller than for AMD chips.
Be prepared for some work installing this fan as you have to install a new back-plate on the motherboard. The included parts are perfect in that they provide everything you will need including the thermal compound. So I also purchased the 2 top case fans (Corsair series). Without the cooler, the top fans did indeed reduce the top CPU temperatures by about 4C degrees - almost as though the case cover is open. With the cooler though the CPU temperature never climbed beyond 61C degrees even when all 8 cores were saturated (was compiling code). Without the cooler and the the top fans I was hitting 70C degrees which is 5 degrees above allowed operating temperature. I am surprised my AMD 8350 is still operational. With the cooler and top fans the temperature drop is 15C which is a win! Maybe I can use the Arcrtic Freezer in an Intel setup.

Polk Audio RC65i 2-way Premium In-Wall 6.5" Speakers, Pair of 2 Perfect for Damp and Humid Indoor/Outdoor Placement - Bath, Kitchen, Covered Porches (White, Paintable-Grille) I was really impressed with how easy these were to install. The user's guide clearly walked me through the process even though these were the first in-wall speakers I've installed. It also comes with a very handy template to ensure it's a "cut once" process with no regrets (or spackle). Since there's a lip on the frame you don't need to be worried about making a perfectly smooth cut through the drywall since the rough edges are hidden.

I was torn between these and the RC80i model. Both had identical tech specs on the Polk site. What sealed the deal in terms of the RC85i model is that it is a bit more shallow than the RC80i (depth of 2 and 7/8 inches for the RC85i versus 3 and 1/4 inches with the RC80i). More importantly, the tweeter assembly on the RC85i is a bit different. According to Polk, the tweeter in the 85i has a plate underneath it that helps project the sound. This is not found in the 80i.

But the proof is in the sound, and these sound wonderful. I'm using them in a basement wired to a Denon AV receiver in the LR. While the sound can't compete with the Kef's I have in the LR, the Polks sound far better than I expected given the price. Very pleased!

They also are very aesthetically pleasing. The grill is nicely made, and can be painted. As with installation, clear and detailed instructions on painting the grills are in the user's guide.

Good sound, good looks and good price - can't ask for more! Highly recommend.

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Wireless Headset for iPad, iPhone and iPod Touch Immediately, I realized I love these headphones. I'm not in love with the color, and I'm perplexed why companies always say something is for iPad, etc., although I suspect it is just the "cool" thing to do. I have no apple devices, but this worked immediately and perfectly for my Blackberry 9700, Xoom, and Win7 Laptop.

The first device pairs by itself, and devices 2-8 pair by holding 2 buttons for 5 seconds. After that, if multiple devices are turned on when you turn the headphones on, it seems to want to pick the first one you paired it with.

The BB picks it up as a Logitech Wireless Headset (not something generic), and you can then control the volume with the BB or with the headset itself (Did I mention the controls are all well positioned on the right headphone? - just two volume buttons, mic mute, micro USB charging port, and LED indicator), and you can also toggle between BB speaker phone and headset - they are obviously fully compatible - not generically. Pressing the mute button give you an audible cue, but does not change the BB display.

You'll never catch me in public with a normal bluetooth earpiece on anyway, so this is also great for calls at home - it will cancel out more background noise (because of the foam on both ears) so you can comfortably concentrate on your call. My tests show it working well more than the claimed 10m away (of course that partly depends on the other device's radio as well).

As another reviewer said, these sound good (and are capable of getting louder than I'll ever need), but are probably not as great as the full over-the-ear headsets. BUT, the wireless capability is really great to keep you fully uninhibited when exercising, cooking, or whatever you're doing when talking on the phone or listening to your music. For the record, I am 100% opposed to wireless shelf/tower speakers in a real home system, but this is a great solution for a headset.

Also, the mic backing out of the way is a must, so thankfully that is included. It not only pivots, but flexes toward or away from the mouth as well - very good design. Finally, the folding feature is great; any space saved is important. And the connecting wire connecting the two sides is accessible, if all that bending ever has it in need of a replacement.

Past helmet use has me thinking my skull is about as large as they come, and these are comfortable on me with the sides fully extended.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Wireless Headset for iPad, iPhone and iPod Touch

text_fidelity_a:
ASUS VS197D-P 18.5" WXGA 1366x768 VGA Back-lit LED Monitor, Black I'm very pleased with this monitor. I needed to replace my second screen and didn't want to spend a lot, but needed a monitor with 1920x1200 resolution. This seemed like a decent bet. It has exceeded my expectations with regard to performance. The clarity is excellent -- it rivals my primary screen which cost three times as much!

The monitor is very lightweight. It comes with both DVI and VGA cables, which was unexpected. I like that there's no power transformer or wall wart. It has just a regular power cord. Set up is simple (just attached the base and no tools are needed).

Of course, at this price point some features are not present. For example, while the screen can be tilted back and forth a bit, it does not have any up/down adjustment, nor can it be swiveled into portrait mode. There's no USB connectors and no speakers. But for me, none of those were deal breakers. I wanted a good quality monitor that was affordable, and this hit the mark 100%. Plus, it does not scrimp on connections. There's DVI, VGA and HDMI. I'm using DVI at present since the PC I'm using it with is a few years old. But, my next PC will probably have a HDMI connection, making this monitor future-proof (well, as future-proof as any tech product can be).

If you're looking for a basic monitor that does not scrimp on image quality, this should definitely be on your short list. Also, check Amazon Warehouse for used ones. I got mine there (it was probably a customer's return). It looks brand new, and only ran me $127.
text_fidelity_b: ASUS VS197D-P 18.5" WXGA 1366x768 VGA Back-lit LED Monitor, Black

text_fidelity_a:
CORSAIR Hydro Series H105 AIO Liquid CPU Cooler, 240mm Thick Radiator, Dual 120mm PWM Fans I've wanted to try one of these liquid CPU coolers for ages, but it always been a little too cheap to spend the extra money on one, and I confess I've been mildly concerned about using a liquid anything inside my computer. I'm glad I tried this out.

This particular model has a radiator style grate which the fan sits on (there is some conductive paste included), then has tubes leading to the cooler unit. The water is totally enclosed in the system, and I can see no danger of leakage. The fan is quiet and unobtrusive.

It has a four pin connector, so if your computer has a four pin connector as well, your computer can control the speed of the fan. However, the four pin connector can also connect to a three pin connector and it works fine, you just lose that extra bit of control.

The one small improvement I'd like to see is that the water/cooling area only goes to one side of the radiator type grate, not around all of the edges, so one side of it will always be hotter than the other. It still disperses heat well, just seems like a less efficient system then it could be.

Lastly, I love the thumbscrews included for installing. I hate dealing with normal screws, and the thumbscrews are such a thoughtful touch that it made me think well of the company for including them.

Overall, if you've been on the fence about testing out one of these new liquid CPU coolers, I don't see any reason not to try out this one. The price is reasonable for what it is, and it looks like a highly effective setup, certainly better than just using a fan.
text_fidelity_b: CORSAIR Hydro Series H105 AIO Liquid CPU Cooler, 240mm Thick Radiator, Dual 120mm PWM Fans

The signal is so weak that it can only load the little icons, showing you the many things you can't see because, the second you click on them, it fails to buffer and the connection times out. Even software and firmware updates, which require relatively little, continually crash. I live in a town house, so the distance for the signal to travel is short; furthermore, all other wi-fi enabled devices work fine and have full signal strength. It is clearly the product. If you are using this to stream video, DO NOT BUY.

They come with a charging case and have a pleasing contemporary appearance. The set include three sets of tips, a charging cable, instructions and safety information. Set up was simple and I had no problem pairing. The buds are on. They are not noise cancelling which is not an issue for my purposes. There is no on off button; they are on once removed from the case. More snniying there is no volume control. You have to adjust using the phone or other device. They fit as comfortablyvas phones of this style can and have performed satisfactorily. Battery life is good, about five hours on a single charge. text_fidelity_a:
Fisher Price Precious Planet Whale of a Tub We purchased this product before we were expecting, knowing that it was neutral gendered and would be perfect for a boy or a girl. When we had our first child, a 9 lb, 11 oz baby girl, I was SO nervous! I didn't know a thing about babies. My eldest sister helped me give her her first bath and complimented our whale tub. She said it was so nice that the green padding in the base would help prevent baby from slipping. By the third bath, I had it down.

As the weeks have gone on, our little one has really loved her tub. She began holding her head up at 4 days old and was doing so independently within a month of her birth. She loved kicking and splashing in her tub. She has never cried in the bath. We use a turtlemeter thermometer and she thinks of it like a little toy with which to play.

I would recommend this tub with the seat in it for a newborn baby up to about 12 lbs. Once our daughter was 13 lbs, she has trouble staying warm in the tub with the seat attached. It simply wasn't deep enough for her while she was lying down and she only got her bottom half wet unless I poured water over her, and the chilly air would then make her cold.

With the seat out, she needs to be sitting on her own so there was a two month gap where we did not use her tub, and instead bathed her with me in the big tub.

Once she was a successful sitter, we returned her to this tub for warmer nights, so she could sit and play in the water. She loves it!

After a bath, I would recommend not only using the drain in the tub, but turning this whale tub upside-down and and then turning it from side-to-side to drain it, as the water tends to get trapped beneath the green padded area. You can also remove the seat to clean under it. Using dish soap and a scrub daddy sponge, I am able to quickly clean the tub in-between uses.
text_fidelity_b: Fisher Price Precious Planet Whale of a Tub

APC Back-UPS Pro 1000VA UPS Battery Backup & Surge Protector (BR1000G) I got this for Christmas and have only been using it for a few days now. I did have a problem with the set-up since there were no step by step instructions and you are left to figure out what goes where. I had omitted attaching the USB/phone jack between my old Windows XP computer and the UPS. I've used UPS's in years past, but they did not require a USB connection to a computer. I found out I had a problem when I was trying to install the software and it stopped loading and gave me a problem message, but no solution. I called the 1-888 number and without any fuss or waiting I got to speak to someone in the tech department who spoke very good English and solved my problem quickly.

I was tempted to deduct one star for the lousy (or total lack of) any instructions on how to connect this to your computer but didn't since the tech help was so good. There was a picture drawing instructing the user to remove the battery and turn it over so the green tape is on top which I managed to do alright. I don't hear any fan noise whatsoever as some others were complaining of. In fact, it's so quiet I can't even tell it's on unless I go and see the 3 LED lights on the top panel.

I tested it out a few minutes ago by turning off the power to the room that my computer is in. I was downstairs in the garage at the fuse box so I don't know if any beep occurred upstairs, but when I got there the computer was running off the UPS. Every 30 seconds I heard 4 beeps from the UPS telling me that it was being used as the power source. I only have my computer, monitor and modem connected to the UPS. I figure I don't need the extra peripheral equipment to stay powered up since it only sucks more energy from my UPS. I didn't wait to see how long the UPS would power my PC but I did sit there for about 3 minutes before I went downstairs and turned the power back on. My computer had a message on the screen saying that it was now being powered by regular current again (or something to that effect).

So far I like this UPS a LOT. There's nothing more frustrating then losing your work if the power goes off for only a couple of seconds. I edit a lot of music and it's not always easy or convenient to save it while I edit it just because of the nature of the program I use. So, I really like the idea of hearing my 4 beeps to let me know I might need to close out and shut down and not lose any work. I don't always have lights on so there may be nothing to tell me there's been a power outage except for the beeps on this UPS. There is a mute mode, but I need to hear the beeps.
text_fidelity_b: APC Back-UPS Pro 1000VA UPS Battery Backup & Surge Protector (BR1000G)

text_fidelity_a:
Inateck 3.5 Hard Drive Enclosure, Aluminum USB 3.0 Sata HDD Enclosure, FE3001 I've had this enclosure for almost 2 years. My five year old computer was very slow and I was having lots of trouble with it and the enclosure connecting to it. I did get it to connect and do one backup, but that was it. So, I thought surely it was my pc that was the problem. It would either not connect or it would not do anything...like I didn't have it plugged in. I just thought all three connections had to be made properly for it to come on and do it's job. I am not completely tech stupid, nor savvy.
I am disabled, so I was saving for a new computer. I have had lots of sickness over this time, and getting to this was not a huge priority and I never came back to read reviews. I wish I had.
I finally did recently get a new pc, and just the other day wanted to give it another go. When I plugged it in, again, there seemed to be no power... and then suddenly there was a burning smell and smoke coming from the enclosure where the power supply went in. It was quite scary, because I almost did not catch it soon enough.
I took a long shot and contacted the company anyways, even though it had been such a while to explain the long ordeal, and why I had not contacted sooner... Among my sickness, I was giving the device the benefit of the doubt, because I honestly thought it was my pc.
This is the message I received in return "In this case, it is highly commended to stop using this hard drive enclosure.
According to your information, this item is faulty. Regarding our products, a 12-month warranty is provided, however, it is obviously that the item ordered on 2016 has been far beyond its warranty. Hope that you could understand."
They did offer a 15% "return after purchase" discount refund if I would purchase a new one. But, as I am disabled, I cannot afford to do that at this time.
Hopefully, my backup really is on the hard drive that this unit supposedly saved it to that one time, as some beloved photos of my deceased father are on there, and I don't have them anywhere else.
I wish I were more tech savvy and didn't stay sick so much... Even so, I wouldn't have known the problem until I got a new pc anyways. Based on my experience and other reviews, I would not recommend this enclosure to anyone.
I do hope this helps someone.
text_fidelity_b: Inateck 3.5 Hard Drive Enclosure, Aluminum USB 3.0 Sata HDD Enclosure, FE3001

text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm Finepix F70EXR 10MP Super CCD Digital Camera with 10x Optical Dual Image Stabilized Zoom and 2.7 inch LCD The Fuji F70 EXR has features which clearly depart from the "same old, just a little better" way of doing things. For one, it puts the camera's digital nature front and center and manipulates images to improve them. Starting with the common auto red eye reduction, extending to pixel binning for high dynamic range or low light shots in EXR mode, as well as merging multiple shots in the natural light flash, pro low light and pro focus modes. Couple such digital magic with a great new sensor and a good zoom lens, packaged into a very small, attractive camera, and you have a real winner. In Auto EXR mode it even switches automatically to macro mode when needed, a feature I wanted for the longest time.

My favorite mode is EXR high dynamic range. On a recent trip through the Southwest US I pretty much left the camera in this mode with the Velvia film simulation (i.e. vivid colors), and all outdoor shots turned out great. Stunning, vivid colors, good detail in highlights and shadows, and nothing overdone. Simply cool!

Originally I bought the F70EXR for low light shots at work because the new sensor and software promised to yield better results than older PnSes, and it does. I have sharp handheld shots without flash that I simply have never been able to take with any other point and shoot (or older SLR for that matter). I alternate between EXR high iso/low noise, natural flash and SP night modes for this, depending on the situation or how much time I have to think and plan.

Overall, this camera is fun to use and gives great pictures almost all of the time.

Pros:
small and light
great auto modes, especially high dynamic range EXR
nice 10x zoom lens - love the range
great sensor, larger than average for PnS
smart software
fast focus and time to shoot
high quality bright display

Cons:
pronounced purple fringing (chromatic aberration) around bright, high contrast edges
finicky zoom lever - I wish it had two levels of sensitivity

Quibbles:
mode wheel turns too easily for me
some modes have overlapping features, makes choices confusing (e.g. Astia film simulation for soft tones vs. two portrait modes which promise soft skin tones)
multi shot modes are impossible if subject doesn't hold absolutely still
on/off button somewhat difficult to find by touch for me
would be nice if the lens defaulted to somewhere between 35 and 50 mm equivalent focal length instead of the very wide angle 27 mm
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm Finepix F70EXR 10MP Super CCD Digital Camera with 10x Optical Dual Image Stabilized Zoom and 2.7 inch LCD

Garmin Forerunner 110 GPS-Enabled Unisex Sport Watch (Black) (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I did a lot of research before making this purchase. I'm training for my first half marathon and wanted something that could track my distance and time, as well as my heart rate...but at the same time I needed it to be very simple. This watch had great reviews across the board.
Each day you run the watch has to reset position (unless you just wear it throughout the day). Do not hit the GPS button until you are outside and clear of your home/building. A couple of times I tried to get a jump start on the watch and hit the button while getting ready inside. My run was off by nearly 200 feet. This may not seem like a lot but when you are running multiple miles it adds up.
As long as you hit the GPS button while outside though you won't have any problems. It was dead on every time when I did this.
The battery life lasts (depending on your distance) about four days with consistent use.
It recharges very quickly so if you run in the morning and at night, you will easily have a full charge prior to your second run...typically takes 3 hours or so for a full charge from completely dead.
Definitely recommend the watch, especially for beginner and intermediate runners.

I was in the market for an inexpensive dual-boot Win10/Android tablet. I researched for about a week, and I am really happy with the choice I made.

What I wanted: A 8 or 10-inch tablet that I could use for web browsing and video streaming. I game and have a nice gaming laptop that I didn't want to lug around for these purposes. I wanted a decent screen that didn't look cheap. Also the ability to play Android games.

This tablet meets all my expectations. Build is solid and feels high quality. Screen is very bright and text is clear. I had no issues getting accounts set up in Android or Win 10. Android is bare bones and has just about nothing pre-installed, which I love. I would absolutely recommend this tablet, especially at this price point.

What you don't get: No video out port. There is a pro version of this tablet if you need that option. You are not doing any major Windows gaming on this. You are not going to run any extremely resource-intensive Windows apps on this. It has a mono speaker so you aren't getting a high-end audio experience with music. If these are things you need, you will have to spend at least six times as much.

USB Power Strip Tower, BESFAN Surge Protector with 12 Outlets and 5 USB Ports, 10ft Extension Cord USB (Desktop Smart Charging Station) for Home, Dorm and Office As most of us know – if we have electronics (laptops, iPads, phones) – we need a surge protector.

And, since about 2003 – I’ve had TONS of them. Even ones that protected the landline cord (do we even have landlines anymore). I’ve had wide/flat, narrow/flat, and just ones that mounted to a wall.

I’ve had ones that didn’t have enough outlets either, or the outlets were spaced just “so” that I couldn’t plug up adapter type plugs (phones, etc). And, ones that the wall cord was so short they didn’t help out much in certain areas.

This one?

WOW! Game changer!

Not only the shape – I would never have thought of a tower design. But, it does save room. I have mine under my desk and with my old flat one – I ended up turning it off countless times. Not this one though. Outlets? 12 outlets which comes in handy, along with five (5) USB ports.

This is a LONG wall cord so plugging it into outlets further/farther away than where you need it is not a huge problem. Unless the outlet is across the room.

The outlets on this unit are spaced and sectioned for big or small plugs. And, the USB ports are a huge bonus! Some devices don’t come with a wall adapter and either you spend money on one, or you have to hook it up to your computer. This? That eliminates that situation.

I can’t attest to others’ and their phones – this charges my phone in the same amount of time as the wall adapter to the USB cord would. So, not much difference there.

Other than the cool stuff, this functions just like other surge protectors. No issues so far. It’s fairly sturdy and I’m definitely glad I got this! I’m definitely sold on this design and I plan to upgrade my household with them as I can.

I definitely wouldn’t hesitate to recommend this. Would make a great “house-warming” gift.

text_fidelity_a:
Roku Express - HD Streaming Player There's already been 980 reviews for this Roku, so I can only support the good things already said about it. I have been using a previous Roku for the last 5 or more years and it worked pretty well most of the time so when this one became available for review I jumped on it - and glad I did!

The Roku Express was fairly easy to install but you have to wait for a lot of updates to download. We patiently waited through 105 updates and some of them had sub-updates. I guess it took about 15 minutes total from hook-up to actually using. It comes with a short HDMI cable and a power cable. You can use a USB port on your television to power it if you have one, otherwise the included power cord works fine. I like having one less cord behind the TV to mess with. Streaming is faster than on the older one, and I can still watch all of my favorite channels - Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, You Tube, etc.... plus a lot of freebie channels. The Roku Express is a lot smaller than my older Roku and I thought the old one was small. It can be attached to the top of your TV and makes it easier to aim the IR remote at it. It still has to be pretty much a direct line of sight to the sensor on the Roku but I haven't had any problems with it.

I've only had the Roku Express for a couple of days but so far I love it. I haven't paid for TV viewing in years (except for the monthly internet service charge and Netflix/and Amazon) and rarely watch regular TV anymore. If I have any problems with it I'll update this review, but for now it's super easy to use and install.
text_fidelity_b: Roku Express - HD Streaming Player

ASUS AC3100 WiFi Router (RT-AC3100) - Dual Band Wireless Internet Router, Trend Micro Lifetime AiProtection, AiMesh Compatible, Parental Control, MU-MIMO ASUS makes excellent routers overall with the added bonus of being compatible with a variety of free-ware router software like DD-WRT, Tomato, and Merlin-WRT (recommended). It includes all of the features you need for a proper home LAN, far better than the junky wireless routers offered by your internet provider, especially Comcast XFinity. (Don't believe the hype- their equipment is terrible.)

Some great features include
- Great 802.11ac support (5 GHz wireless support)
- Legacy 802.11b support (2.4 Ghz wireless support used in most cheap IOT devices)
- DHCP support which includes local DNS and MAC ID binding to make NAT and Firewall rules effective with having to manually configure your devices with easy to use client management
- Easy to use QOS with instrumentation features
- VPN support
- Many storage solution variants to allow for of personal cloud and LAN network storage (NAS-like functionality)
- Gaming networking enhancements galore
- Excellent security features
- Excellent compatibility with other devices
- Excellent and easy to use web-base administration software
- Excellent community support on countless on-line forums
- Best router for the money; Similarly featured Netgear routers are significantly more expensive without a real edge

Some downsides:
- Terrible vendor support (not really necessary unless you need a warranty replacement, but they are okay here)
- Some software limitations make many features will only work when you use local subnets within the 192.168.0.0/16 class B network
- Network storage throughput somewhat slow

It is devices like this that have had me a loyal ASUS customer for routers for nearly a decade. The fact that you can use Merlin-WRT as your software which IMHO more stable than the factory firmware makes it a slam-dunk.
text_fidelity_b: ASUS AC3100 WiFi Router (RT-AC3100) - Dual Band Wireless Internet Router, Trend Micro Lifetime AiProtection, AiMesh Compatible, Parental Control, MU-MIMO

text_fidelity_a:
Amcrest ProHD 1080P WiFi 2MP (1920TVL) Indoor Pan/Tilt Security Wireless IP Camera IP2M-841B (Black) UPDATE:
The whole purpose of having a WiFi camera is to put it up in the best place and have it connect via, duh, WiFi.

After finally figuring out how to do that (plug it in temporarily with an ethernet cable, get it to connect via WiFi, then disconnect and relocate the camera) I got it to work. For about a week. For some reason, it "forgets" it's supposed to be on a WiFi network and after a few days simply stops sending the picture to my phone. If I unplug the camera from the wall and reboot, it auto-reconnects, but after a few days, it falls off the network again.

I won't buy another.

Original review:
I received the Amcrest ProHD 1080p IP PT "WiFi" camera yesterday, 10/30/15.

I downloaded the Amcrest Lite iPhone app. Followed instructions. It would not connect via Wi-Fi using my router's password. Tried again and again. I have a TP-Link C9 dual band wireless router with both 5gHz and 2.4gHz transmission. The Amcrest website says in an obscure forum post that the camera operates only in the 2.4gHz band. I changed my iPhone6 (iOS 9.0.2) from 5G to 2.4G. Still could connect via Wi-Fi.

So I plugged the camera directly into the router via ethernet, completely defeating the purpose for the initial purchase. It finally connected. I saw the picture for about 30 seconds, trying to get the camera to full screen, I clicked around on the mysterious icons. Nothing seemed to work. I clicked on the "X" box. The camera disappeared. I tried to reconnect. It came back with "USER LOCKED." I went to their website to search for an answer. They said (at least for their DVR line -- virtually nothing was about this camera) "users are locked out after two failed logon attempts and that I must wait 30 minutes for the reset." I waited. Still USER LOCKED. No camera. I don't even recall trying to log in. I was in the app, trying to reconnect the camera.

I created my Amcrest user account and received their confirming email. I created a user and password for Amcrest.com. The account is actually for something called amcrest.Zendesk and Accumed.zendesk and Foscamhelp.zendesk. I then tried to log in at Amcrest.com. It won't take my log-on credentials. "Invalid Logon or Password." How many user names and passwords does it take to plug in a camera?

Trying to start over, I deleted the app and rebooted the camera. Still USER LOCKED.

Finally, I found that if you push and hold in the little LED network-activity-indicator button on the back of the camera for 10 seconds, the camera will reset to factory. Deleted the app again, set my phone to operate in the 2.4gHz band. Still won't connect via WiFi. Plugged in via ethernet, then used my router's password and it connected. Per the prompt, I then created a new secure password, replacing the default "admin/admin". Finally, I can see and control the camera. So, I have a WiFi camera that won't WiFi. The camera needs to connect to the router at 2.4gHz band (and in my case, via an ethernet cable) but after getting it set, the phone can go back to the 5G if desired.

They claim their products are "Simple, Reliable, Secure." Not quite. They fail to hook to Wi-Fi and then lock me out. Their website won't let me log on even with a user and password.

I downloaded the camera's big PDF user manual to find what the icons mean. The document looks nothing like the camera's icons. They went into great detail...about a previous firmware version, then changed the firmware to look very differently.

The camera works, eventually, and only via ethernet in some cases, but getting there is a real test of patience.
text_fidelity_b: Amcrest ProHD 1080P WiFi 2MP (1920TVL) Indoor Pan/Tilt Security Wireless IP Camera IP2M-841B (Black)

Foldable Bluetooth Keyboard, Geyes Folding Wireless Keyboard with Portable Pocket Size, Aluminum Alloy Housing, Carrying Pouch, for iPad, iPhone, and More Tablets, Laptops and Smartphones(Gold) This folding keyboard is a bit of a betwixt and between product, but if it is the sort of thing you think you might use, then it’s got a lot to like about it. If you have a tablet (and my experience is with iPads so keep that in mind), then their built in keyboard is a better choice for short work just because it’s larger and more natural to type. For longer work, the choice will be more individual in that some people hate writing for extended time on the hard surface of a tablet keyboard and others don’t mind at all. I can do a pretty long stint and for really long work, I’ll shift over to a Bluetooth keyboard, either Apple’s own or a smaller Logitech one that also acts as a cover. I’d prefer both of those to this because again, they are larger and so more comfortable.

When one considers the keyboard as a phone accessory, then things change a bit, and this become a much more viable choice. If I have to do any halfway extensive typing on a phone for work (something beyond texting, an email or two, etc., then this would definitely be my preference over the phone itself.

1) it takes up very little space (and comes with a nice little pouch). Tossing it into a backpack is nothing, but I could easily fit it into a coat pocket, a cargo pants-like pocket, keep it in my car console without it blocking much space. None of which would be true for my wireless Apple keyboard or even my slimmer Logitech one. The additional “bulk” is therefore relatively negligible.

2) the typing is quite nice on it. I was pleasantly surprised at the key travel, the ease, the tactile sense.

3) It’s definitely small and a little cramped, but not so I notice it unless I’m typing for a long time (half hour or more) and then I just need to take a few minutes break. The small size doesn’t come into play too often. I had to readjust to the apostrophe, and one has to hunt and seek a bit for less-used keys, but that’s easy enough and once you’ve been typing for a while it becomes just as second nature as normal typing does. And it’s much faster and much more comfortable than extensive phone typing

4) the stand is a nice little touch that works quite well, placing the phone at a usable and pleasant working angle and letting you sue it in both portrait and landscape mode.

5) I haven’t exhausted the battery so can’t speak to how long it will go, but it’s certainly lasted a good number of hours, more than I’d ever use it for (if I’m working that long I’m going to my laptop or tablet)

6). Build quality seems sufficient. I wouldn’t say it feels highly durable, but nor would I call it cheap feeling or overly flimsy. And when it’s folded I have no concerns about it breaking.

text_fidelity_a:
Western Digital 3TB WD Purple Surveillance Internal Hard Drive HDD - SATA 6 Gb/s, 64 MB Cache, 3.5" - WD30PURZ I purchased this as a data storage/backup drive for my desktop PC. My main drive is a1TB NVME drive. The data drive I use for movies, songs, and backups and digital images. Since I am not booting with the drive I don't care about raw performance, nor will I pay for it. With that said I am VERY happy with this drive. It only spins at 5400 RPM, so the access time is slightly slower, but it makes no difference to me. Maximum transfer rate is nearly 200MB/sec. High capacity drives have dense platters and are able to pull data faster.

I am a Nazi for eliminating extraneous sound and used to keep my drives inside enclosures to reduce sound. My quietest drive to date is the Samsung HD 503HI, and this is even quieter. I have several large case fans spinning slowly and if I turn them off I can ever so slightly hear a faint humming or click, but otherwise I hear NOTHING.

This is my first WD drive (have always used Samsung). I cannot speak to the drive's reliability as I've only had it for one month. It is labeled for "Surveillance," so if it's meant to be running 24/7- 365 it is meant to get use in commercial/industrial environments.

I think everyone with a desktop PC should adopt this system. It is very easy to backup anything important- save it to your C: drive as well as your backup E: drive or whatever. If one your main drive goes kaput you have the backup to pull your saved data from. You can use flash drives for additional redundancy and portability, but in my experience they are not so reliable.
text_fidelity_b: Western Digital 3TB WD Purple Surveillance Internal Hard Drive HDD - SATA 6 Gb/s, 64 MB Cache, 3.5" - WD30PURZ

But this FiiO is like the candle you burn from both ends, you know, twice the light but half the time. This thing will drive ANY IEM’s you have to ear bleeding levels and when you look you’re at 45, OUT OF 100 on the volume scale. And while I am an IEM guy I do own a pair of HiFiMan HE-400i planars and I rarely see anything above 55 on the volume with it on Hi Gain. I only run 2.5mm balanced so the battery usually taps out after about 5-6 hours. Not bad, but not the ES100’s 10 hours. But the power, man this sucker punches way above it’s weight. I use it mainly with my Samsung Galaxy phone and strictly LDAP. Everything else is disabled in the software/app that FiiO provides. And that is my second gripe. The ES100 rules on the app side. If FiiO put some time and money into providing similar functionality into their red headed stepchild app they could ask twice the price and I’d still think it was a bargain. But all the gripes aside it is definitely a step up from the ES100. Some told me if you have the Radsone that you’re good to go, no need to buy the FiiO. Fiddlesticks, BahHumbug and all those other quaking aphorisms. Buy it. It will make you smile.

However, after getting this external drive kit and setting it up with a SamSung 970 EVO NVME drive and updating to the latest JMC firmware, it worked okay for Windows workloads but it had serious problems with Linux on a Raspberry Pi 4B. tons of UAS reset errors. Additionally, the drive gets really hot with use. hot to the touch and almost worrisome. I know this may be somewhat normal for NVME drive enclosures but it definitely feels above my personal safety threshold.

I'm going to try a different drive enclosure next with the RTL9210 chipset as I've read more favorable reviews on that.

text_fidelity_a:
Phaiser BHS-750 Bluetooth Headphones Headset Sport Earphones with Mic and Lifetime Sweatproof Guarantee - Wireless Earbuds for Running, Redheat 3-day update: After trying many tips I'm still not overly impressed. I found I got the best fit with the wire over rear but the mic keeps them from being practical over-ear and the angle of the wire on the other side with the tip at the best angle for kept making the wire come off my ear. In not a fan of comply tips but I finally tried them as a last resort and the sound did improve. But in the end, my theory is that I just can't get these deep enough in my ear due to the large housing to get some bass to balance out the brightness. But even if it did I find the mid-range to lack warmth and certain aspect of the sound to be harsh.

First impression - not as impressed as some

Disclaimer: Everyone's ear is different, and tips make a big difference. Because of my ears, I have to use big tips and a shallow fit. Those who can get a deeper fit my hear something completely different. Also, I'm being really picky to help others decide if this is the right phones for them.

I wanted to try these on my computer because that is where all my music is stored that I've used for decades to audition audio gear. So this will be based on Pandora on my phone at 192kb. This is fine because this is how I will be listening to them.

I could not get a comfortable fit with the included tips. The largest tips were not large enough for my ears. So I dug through my collection and found a good fit. Pairing went fine.

They feel a little heavy to me but maybe that is the price of Bluetooth and the magnets? This is my first pair of Bluetooth in-ears. Build quality seem good for the price (I got them on sale) and I'd say the build quality is about average for their normal selling price. While they look like they have good strain relief it's actually very stiff plastic creating a 'hard point' where the wires come out. I like the little magnet for when I want to take them out but not take them off. It's one of the reasons I got these. If you run, I'd worry a little bit about the weight they add.

The sound. I like tight bass, well controlled, no extra bloom/extension But these are bass shy to my ears. For a workout, I like a fun sound and these ain't that. They are a bit bright and brassy at times I noticed the most on 70s classic rock. They lack a richness in the mids that I noticed most with male vocals. Turning them up did not improve they sound, as they got louder they became painful bright/brassy and bass did not improve. They went loud enough to distort the drivers so volume should not be an issue for anyone.

They do a pretty good job of revealing detail and room acoustics are rendered decently and there is some space around the instruments but not much of a soundstage.

While not sterile they lack some musicality that I'd prefer. Did I mention that male voice sound thin. They lack a fullness and resonance for the male voice. I notice this lack of 'something' on drums as well which are buried in the mix. It seems like the SQ is geared to making them sound impressive and accurate and while they succeed in that to some extent it's at the expense of other parts of the sound. I can see getting some fatigue after a while if you listen for more than an hour or so. Sibilance is not an issue. You hear the sibilance on some songs because it's there but it's not going to wear you out.

I can see why some people would like these especially if you are coming from lower quality mushy sounding earphones. If you are used to better earphones and looking for some less expensive earphones for working out you may like these if you like a 'clear' sound but the word that keeps coming to mind as I listen to them more and more is 'thin'. Not thin/thin but a lack of richness and resonance. If you want some bass especially some extension/bloom (again wearing/tips can make a difference) and a bit of 'drive' I'd consider a different set.
text_fidelity_b: Phaiser BHS-750 Bluetooth Headphones Headset Sport Earphones with Mic and Lifetime Sweatproof Guarantee - Wireless Earbuds for Running, Redheat

text_fidelity_a:
Contour +2 - Old Packaging (Discontinued by Manufacturer) This is a really cool camera in a lot of ways, and yet there are two things about it that I hate:

1) It writes *.mov files. Why would any company choose that over so many great standards out there? Quicktime is the norm for *.mov files, with other players claiming to play them, but often with issues. Quicktime is one of those programs that - even after you uninstall it and delete everything you can find associated with it in your registry - will hound you until the end of your days to upgrade and constantly ask permission to take over your computer, will change other file extensions to play on it without asking, etc. Therefore, I so loathe Quicktime that I generally won't even touch an *.mov file.

I'd even be tempted to take the product down to three stars because of this, but there is some chance that this was the only format that would allow them to include the GPS data. I sort of doubt it because Apple (Quicktime) is the most ridiculously proprietary company I can think of, but I guess I need to give Contour the benefit of the doubt. Same benefit of the doubt used for annoyance #2:

2) You need to install more software to see the GPS data. I hate installing more and more software on my computer because everything installed is just another chance to have something running as a service or process all the time, wasting your resources. In general, all software is more "bloated" than ever these days, making our more powerful than before computers unable to perform better than before.

I also wish for some Blackberry support, but they might have some with BB OS 10, supposedly. Frankly, I'm not that interested in the smart phone features; they just slow you down.

As I said, the camera is really cool, though, for its ease of use and its mounts. It's obviously geared toward adventurers and people that want to roll off roofs in shopping carts like that one show that used to be popular. It has a great feel to it in its construction and durability, but I want to make clear the very big caveat that these are the only reasons you want this camera. Besides the annoyances mentioned above, I have a couple point and shoot cameras that do 1080p video just as well (actually better, given their native formats) and they are smaller and cost less. But it is pretty awesome to mount this on your bike for those "just in case" scenarios.
text_fidelity_b: Contour +2 - Old Packaging (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a:
Display Port to HDMI Converter with Audio Adapter I wanted to hear and see Skype on our Sony XBR7 HDMI-only capable 1080p TV, fed from a Lenovo X220 convertable laptop/tablet running System 7 64 bit Ultimate through the DisplayPort. I also wanted to watch some YouTube videos playing from Firefox and hear their audio on my big living room audio system. No such luck.

When first plugged in, I remember briefly seeing the TV via this DisplayPort adapter in the audio device list, but the next time, the TV disappeared and is nowhere to be found. Not in the audio control panel, anyway. It's just gone.

I first chalked this up to the Thinkpad weirdness, as its internal audio card/mic doesn't work with Skype either. If I plug in an external Logitech webcam, it works seamlessly. Internal camera/mic, nothing.

Sony audio problems aside, the video looks great on the big screen, though it overscans a bit and cuts off part of the menu bar at the bottom.

One reviewer said he could see his TV in the list of audio devices and was able to configure its audio to satisfaction. My Sony TV does not show in the Lenovo audio devices list, though it does show as a generic PnP monitor.

I plugged the HDMI cable into a tiny 7" video monitor and whatdayaknow, the audio came through and the device showed up as an audio device. Then I plugged it into a 20" Vizio and sure enough, it works fine too. Same with a Samsung LCD. Three monitors out of four work. The Sony is the only one that doesn't. Hmmmm.

Sooooo, I'm guessing there's something about Sony's DRM or some other HDMI protocol blocking the computer from seeing the TV. I set all the TVs for internal speakers. Routing audio to an external amp is another variable in the equation.

Nothing wrong with the adapter that I can tell, it simply doesn't see certain Sony TV's.
text_fidelity_b: Display Port to HDMI Converter with Audio Adapter
